questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: Select all three main types of rock.
questions.hint: Three categories — formed by cooling, layering, and changing.
questions.explanation: The three main types are igneous (from cooled magma), sedimentary (compressed layers), and metamorphic (changed by heat and pressure).
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 4 Rocks, Climate, Universe

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: How are igneous rocks formed?
options: By cooling and solidifying of magma or lava
By heat and pressure changing existing rocks
questions.answer: By cooling and solidifying of magma or lava
questions.hint: Think volcanoes.
questions.explanation: Igneous rocks form when hot molten rock (magma underground or lava on the surface) cools and crystallises. Examples: granite (slow-cooled, large crystals), basalt (fast-cooled, small crystals).
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 4 Rocks, Climate, Universe

further_learning.title: Atoms, Elements and Compounds – Oak National Academy
KS3 Science – BBC Bitesize

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: How are sedimentary rocks formed?
options: By layers of sediment being compacted and cemented over time
By heat and pressure deep underground
questions.answer: By layers of sediment being compacted and cemented over time
questions.hint: Layers settle on top of each other and squash down.
questions.explanation: Sedimentary rocks form when sediment (rock fragments, shells, organic matter) settles in layers, gets buried, and is compressed and cemented over millions of years. Examples: sandstone, limestone, chalk.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 4 Rocks, Climate, Universe

further_learning.title: Atoms, Elements and Compounds – Oak National Academy
KS3 Science – BBC Bitesize

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: How are metamorphic rocks formed?
options: By heat and pressure changing existing rocks (without melting)
questions.answer: By heat and pressure changing existing rocks (without melting)
questions.hint: 'Meta-' means 'changed'.
questions.explanation: Metamorphic rocks form when existing rocks are squashed and heated (but not melted) deep underground. The minerals rearrange. Examples: limestone → marble, mudstone → slate.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 4 Rocks, Climate, Universe

further_learning.title: Atoms, Elements and Compounds – Oak National Academy
KS3 Science – BBC Bitesize

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: Marble is formed from which original rock under heat and pressure?
questions.hint: Both contain calcium carbonate.
questions.explanation: Limestone (sedimentary) is changed by heat and pressure into marble (metamorphic). Marble has larger interlocking crystals, which is why it's harder and used in sculpture.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 4 Rocks, Climate, Universe

further_learning.title: Atoms, Elements and Compounds – Oak National Academy
KS3 Science – BBC Bitesize

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: Slate is formed from which original rock?
questions.hint: Slate is flaky and splits into thin layers — formed from compacted mud.
questions.explanation: Slate is a metamorphic rock formed from mudstone or shale being squashed. It splits into flat layers, which is why it's used for roof tiles.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 4 Rocks, Climate, Universe

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: Order the steps in the rock cycle that turn igneous rock into sedimentary rock.
options: Compaction and cementation form sedimentary rock
Weathering breaks igneous rock into smaller pieces
Sediment is deposited in layers (often in water)
answer: Weathering breaks igneous rock into smaller pieces
Sediment is deposited in layers (often in water)
Compaction and cementation form sedimentary rock
questions.hint: Weathering → erosion → deposition → compaction.
questions.explanation: Rock cycle steps: weathering (breakdown), erosion (transport), deposition (settling), compaction and cementation (compressing into solid rock). All over millions of years.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 4 Rocks, Climate, Universe

further_learning.title: Atoms, Elements and Compounds – Oak National Academy
KS3 Science – BBC Bitesize

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: What is the difference between weathering and erosion?
options: Weathering breaks rock down in place; erosion moves the pieces away
Weathering happens in winter; erosion in summer
Weathering is fast; erosion is slow
questions.answer: Weathering breaks rock down in place; erosion moves the pieces away
questions.hint: One is breaking; the other is moving.
questions.explanation: Weathering is the breakdown of rock where it sits (by water, wind, ice, plants or chemicals). Erosion is the transport of those weathered pieces by wind, water or ice.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 4 Rocks, Climate, Universe

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: What is freeze-thaw weathering?
options: Water freezing in cracks, expanding and breaking the rock apart
questions.answer: Water freezing in cracks, expanding and breaking the rock apart
questions.hint: Water expands by about 9% when it freezes — what happens to a crack it's sitting in?
questions.explanation: Water gets into a crack, freezes, expands and forces the crack wider. Repeated cycles break chunks of rock off. Common in cold mountainous areas.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 4 Rocks, Climate, Universe

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: Acid rain is a form of which type of weathering?
questions.hint: It's a chemical reaction — acid reacting with the rock.
questions.explanation: Acid rain reacts chemically with rocks like limestone (calcium carbonate), dissolving them away. This is chemical weathering — the rock's composition changes.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 4 Rocks, Climate, Universe

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: In which type of rock are fossils most commonly found?
questions.hint: Fossils need to be preserved gently in layers — heat and pressure destroy them.
questions.explanation: Sedimentary rocks form gradually from layers, so dead organisms get buried and preserved. Igneous and metamorphic rocks involve heat that destroys fossils.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 4 Rocks, Climate, Universe

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: What is the difference between weather and climate?
options: Weather is day-to-day conditions; climate is the average pattern over many years
Weather is hot; climate is cold
Weather is in cities; climate is in the countryside
questions.answer: Weather is day-to-day conditions; climate is the average pattern over many years
questions.hint: Climate is the long-term average.
questions.explanation: Weather: short-term conditions (today, this week). Climate: long-term pattern of weather in a region (typically averaged over 30+ years).
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 4 Rocks, Climate, Universe

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: What is the greenhouse effect?
options: Gases in the atmosphere trapping heat from the Sun
The hole in the ozone layer
questions.answer: Gases in the atmosphere trapping heat from the Sun
questions.hint: Without it, Earth would be far too cold. Too much of it warms the planet.
questions.explanation: The Sun's energy reaches Earth and warms the surface. Earth radiates infrared back, but greenhouse gases (CO2, methane, water vapour) trap some of it, keeping Earth warm. More gases = more warming.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 4 Rocks, Climate, Universe

further_learning.title: Climate Change and Living Sustainably – Oak National Academy
KS3 Science – BBC Bitesize

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: Which of these are greenhouse gases?
questions.hint: Three of them trap infrared radiation. Oxygen, nitrogen and helium don't.
questions.explanation: Main greenhouse gases: water vapour (most common), CO2, methane, nitrous oxide. Oxygen and nitrogen are the bulk of the atmosphere but don't absorb infrared, so they aren't greenhouse gases.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 4 Rocks, Climate, Universe

further_learning.title: Climate Change and Living Sustainably – Oak National Academy
KS3 Science – BBC Bitesize

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: Which human activities contribute to climate change?
questions.hint: Anything that releases CO2 or removes the trees that absorb it.
questions.explanation: Fossil fuel burning releases CO2. Deforestation removes trees that absorb CO2. Petrol cars and coal power are major sources. Recycling and walking REDUCE emissions.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 4 Rocks, Climate, Universe

further_learning.title: Climate Change and Living Sustainably – Oak National Academy
KS3 Science – BBC Bitesize

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT a consequence of climate change?
questions.hint: Three are real climate impacts; one is impossible.
questions.explanation: Climate change causes melting ice, sea level rise, more extreme weather (heatwaves, storms, floods), and habitat loss. Gravity isn't affected by climate.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 4 Rocks, Climate, Universe

further_learning.title: Climate Change and Living Sustainably – Oak National Academy
KS3 Science – BBC Bitesize

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: Which process removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere?
questions.hint: Plants absorb CO2 to make food.
questions.explanation: Plants take in CO2 during photosynthesis: CO2 + water → glucose + oxygen. They're an important carbon sink. Respiration, burning and volcanoes all RELEASE CO2.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 4 Rocks, Climate, Universe

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: What gas makes up about 78% of the Earth's atmosphere?
questions.hint: It's not the one we breathe in for respiration.
questions.explanation: Earth's atmosphere is roughly 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, 0.9% argon, 0.04% carbon dioxide, plus water vapour and trace gases.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 4 Rocks, Climate, Universe

questions.prompt: Approximately what percentage of the atmosphere is oxygen?

questions.prompt: Order the planets from CLOSEST to FURTHEST from the Sun.
questions.hint: Mnemonic: My Very Educated Mother Just Served Us Noodles.
questions.explanation: From the Sun outwards: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune. The first four are rocky; the outer four are gas/ice giants.

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: What is at the centre of our solar system?
questions.hint: Everything else orbits it.
questions.explanation: The Sun is the star at the centre of our solar system. Planets, asteroids and comets orbit it, held by its gravity.

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: What is the Sun?
questions.hint: It produces its own light.
questions.explanation: The Sun is a star — a giant ball of mostly hydrogen and helium, releasing energy by nuclear fusion. It's a fairly average star, just much closer than the others.

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: What is the difference between a planet and a star?
options: Stars produce their own light; planets only reflect it
Stars are made of rock; planets are made of gas
questions.answer: Stars produce their own light; planets only reflect it
questions.hint: Why does Venus shine in the sky?
questions.explanation: Stars produce light and heat by nuclear fusion. Planets don't — they only shine because they reflect light from a nearby star (our Sun, for the planets we see).

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: What is gravity?
options: An attractive force between all objects with mass
questions.answer: An attractive force between all objects with mass
questions.hint: Anything with mass pulls on anything else with mass.
questions.explanation: Gravity is an attractive force between any two objects with mass. The bigger the mass, the stronger the pull. The Earth pulls you down because it's huge.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 4 Rocks, Climate, Universe

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: What keeps the planets in orbit around the Sun?
questions.hint: The Sun has by far the largest mass in the solar system.
questions.explanation: The Sun's huge mass produces a strong gravitational pull on the planets, holding them in orbit. Without gravity, they'd fly off in straight lines.

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: What is the difference between mass and weight?
options: Mass is how much matter you contain (kg); weight is the force of gravity on you (N)
Weight is in kg; mass is in N
questions.answer: Mass is how much matter you contain (kg); weight is the force of gravity on you (N)
questions.hint: Mass stays the same on the Moon; weight doesn't.
questions.explanation: Mass is the amount of matter in an object — same everywhere, measured in kg. Weight is the force gravity exerts on that mass, measured in newtons. weight = mass × gravitational field strength.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 4 Rocks, Climate, Universe

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: Bertie has a mass of 50 kg. Earth's gravitational field strength is 10 N/kg. What is Bertie's weight on Earth (in newtons)?
questions.hint: weight = mass × g
questions.explanation: weight = mass × g = 50 × 10 = 500 N. On the Moon (g ≈ 1.6 N/kg) Bertie's weight would be only 80 N, but mass is still 50 kg.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 4 Rocks, Climate, Universe

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: An object has a mass of 4 kg. The Moon's gravitational field strength is 1.6 N/kg. What is its weight on the Moon (in N)?
questions.hint: weight = mass × gravitational field strength.
questions.explanation: weight = 4 × 1.6 = 6.4 N. Notice the much smaller gravity on the Moon — that's why astronauts can bounce around.

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: What causes day and night?
options: The Sun moving across the sky
questions.hint: Earth turns once every 24 hours.
questions.explanation: Earth rotates on its axis once every 24 hours. The side facing the Sun has day; the side facing away has night.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 4 Rocks, Climate, Universe

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: What causes the seasons?
options: Earth getting closer to the Sun in summer
The tilt of Earth's axis as it orbits the Sun
questions.answer: The tilt of Earth's axis as it orbits the Sun
questions.hint: It's NOT about distance — it's about angle.
questions.explanation: Earth's axis is tilted at about 23.5°. As Earth orbits, different hemispheres tilt towards the Sun at different times. Tilted towards = summer (Sun higher in sky, longer days). Tilted away = winter.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 4 Rocks, Climate, Universe

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: When it is summer in the UK, what season is it in Australia?
questions.hint: Australia is in the Southern Hemisphere, tilted the opposite way.
questions.explanation: When the Northern Hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun (summer in UK), the Southern Hemisphere is tilted away (winter in Australia). The seasons are reversed.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 4 Rocks, Climate, Universe

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: Roughly how long does the Moon take to orbit the Earth once?
questions.hint: Where does the word 'month' come from?
questions.explanation: The Moon orbits Earth about every 27.3 days. This is also why we see a cycle of moon phases (full → new → full) roughly once a month.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 4 Rocks, Climate, Universe

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: Why do we see different phases of the Moon?
options: We see different amounts of the lit half as the Moon orbits Earth
The Earth's shadow always falls on it
questions.answer: We see different amounts of the lit half as the Moon orbits Earth
questions.hint: The Moon doesn't change — but our view of its sunlit side does.
questions.explanation: Half the Moon is always lit by the Sun. As the Moon orbits Earth, we see different fractions of that lit half — full moon (we see all of it), new moon (we see none), and crescents in between.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 4 Rocks, Climate, Universe

questions.prompt: What is the name of the galaxy we live in?
questions.hint: You can see it as a faint band of stars across the night sky.
questions.explanation: The Milky Way is our galaxy — a spiral galaxy containing 100+ billion stars, including our Sun. The Universe contains billions of galaxies.

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: Astronomers use which unit, equal to the distance light travels in a year, to measure huge distances in space?
questions.hint: Two words — it's a distance, not a time, despite the name.
questions.explanation: A light year is the distance light travels in one year — about 9.46 × 10¹⁵ m. Even the nearest star to the Sun (Proxima Centauri) is 4.2 light years away.

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: Roughly how old is the Universe?
questions.hint: Billions, not millions. The Universe began with the Big Bang.
questions.explanation: The Universe is about 13.8 billion years old. It began with the Big Bang and has been expanding ever since. Earth, by comparison, is only 4.5 billion years old.

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: Which of these would help reduce a person's carbon footprint?
options: Driving an electric car charged from renewable electricity
Walking or cycling for short trips
Using public transport instead of driving alone
answer: Driving an electric car charged from renewable electricity
Walking or cycling for short trips
Using public transport instead of driving alone
questions.hint: Choose the options that REDUCE fossil fuel use.
questions.explanation: Reducing fossil-fuel use cuts CO2. Renewable-powered EVs, local food (less transport), active travel, and shared transport all help. Coal burning and leaving lights on increase emissions.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 4 Rocks, Climate, Universe

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: Which energy sources are renewable?
questions.hint: Renewable = never runs out / replaces itself.
questions.explanation: Solar, wind and hydro are renewable — they come from natural processes that won't run out. Coal, oil and gas are fossil fuels — finite, and release CO2 when burned.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 4 Rocks, Climate, Universe
